title: Keep the build moving
hook: Your agents fit on the machine. Your build never starts. Decide what deserves capacity, then write and inspect the scheduler yourself.

scenes.title: A useful machine, a stuck build
scenes.narration: A developer runs browser agents and builds on the same machine. Small agent tasks keep finding spare capacity, while a build waits for enough CPU and memory together. Buying another machine might hide the problem. First work out who is waiting and what guarantee they actually need.

scenes.title: Start with the person waiting
scenes.narration: In his reaction to Michael Hoff, ThePrimeagen describes researching Slurm and Kubernetes before designing local and global job queues. Hoff describes the shift toward supervising agents. Both leave you with a practical question: can you explain why the work an agent produced deserves to run?

scenes.title: Read before you design
scenes.narration: Open the scheduling documents and look for how a waiting job gets a future start time. Find the difference between deciding what fits and deciding what wins. Write your own answers before revealing the reference. Today uses one machine so the decision is small enough to inspect.

scenes.title: Make a claim you can break
scenes.narration: You will review an intentionally flawed proposal, then implement a deterministic scheduler with CPU and memory accounting. Export its real inputs and decision as JSON. Your final note should give another engineer a short way to reproduce the behavior. The weekly project asks whether this policy helps a real workload.

items: A state snapshot from the real code

problem.context: You share a 4-CPU, 8-GB worker between browser agents and builds. A build needs all 4 CPUs for 5 minutes. A stream of 1-CPU agents keeps arriving. The build has waited 40 minutes; developers cannot test their change.
problem.question: What is the best first problem to solve?

options.text: Rewrite the worker in Rust to reduce process overhead.
options.why: Lower overhead might help later. It gives the waiting build no start-time guarantee.

options.text: Measure build wait time and add a capacity reservation before expanding the system.
options.why: This targets the developer delay and gives you a behavior you can test on the current machine.

options.text: Buy a dedicated build worker immediately.
options.why: Isolation can be a good choice if delays cost more than a worker. First measure that tradeoff and check your budget.

cost.q: Assume a worker costs $40/day. A scheduler change costs 3 engineer-hours at $80/hour and saves 20 engineer-minutes each workday. Ignoring maintenance, when does the change repay its engineering cost?
cost.why: $240 divided by $26.67 saved per workday is about 9 workdays. The dedicated worker would cost more per day than this measured saving.

research.guide: Read the named sections yourself. Trace a running job, a waiting large job and a short new job. Write down which event frees both CPU and memory. Do not ask a model to summarize the pages before you try.

questions.q: What must remain true when Slurm starts lower-priority work, and why does its estimate depend on runtime information?
questions.answer: Starting the smaller job must preserve the expected start of higher-priority work. The scheduler needs a credible view of when occupied resources become free. A task that runs past its declared duration can break that prediction.
points: Runtime estimates affect whether a reservation can be honored.

questions.q: Which waiting time increases the Slurm age factor? Does merely submitting a job make its age grow?
questions.answer: Age tracks time spent eligible to run. Waiting on an unfinished dependency does not increase it. The exercise below uses a simpler unbounded score based on submitted time; that is a teaching policy, not Slurm’s complete priority calculation.
points: Eligible waiting time differs from dependency waiting.
Our exercise policy is a simplification of the real scheduler.

questions.q: Why does Kubernetes filter before scoring? What happens if a high-scoring candidate cannot satisfy the resource request?
questions.answer: Filtering removes nodes that cannot run the pod. Scoring ranks the remaining feasible nodes. A preferred node without sufficient resources cannot become valid through a higher score; if no candidate survives filtering, the pod stays unscheduled.
points: Feasibility must be established before preference.

design.prompt: Design one scheduling tick for this worker. In at most 150 words explain capacity, fairness, the reservation and observable state. Include your state transitions. Keep the distributed claim/retry problem as a separate next step.

fields.label: Capacity and ordering
fields.hint: What fits? How does waiting affect priority?

fields.label: States and transitions
fields.hint: queued → reserved or running → finished; what happens on failure?

fields.label: Evidence and failure boundary
fields.hint: What snapshot and test would convince you?

design.coachFocus: Resource accounting; reservations; duplicate execution after a worker crash. Distinguish this single-machine policy from distributed execution.
design.reference: Filter impossible requests and leave future arrivals out. Order eligible jobs by the stated age-adjusted priority. Account for CPU and RAM across running tasks and every task started this tick. Reserve the first blocked job at the earliest release event where both resources fit; accept later tasks only when they finish by that reservation. Emit the inputs and the real plan as JSON. A real worker also needs atomic claims, leases, idempotent side effects and a runtime-overrun policy.
rubric: Both CPU and RAM are accounted for cumulatively.
The first blocked job gets a reservation that backfill cannot move.
Waiting affects priority; tie-breaking is deterministic.
The snapshot is produced by the same code that makes the decision.
Distributed claims and overruns are stated as additional work.

review.intro: This is a planted review exercise. An agent proposes the following design for multiple workers. Decide which claims need correction before it can ship.

artifact.title: Agent proposal
artifact.body:
for job in sorted(queue, key=lambda j: -j.priority):
    if job.cpu <= free_cpu:
        start(job)  # each worker independently reads the global queue

# No reservations: any small job that fits should run.
# Jobs are trusted to finish on time; there is no runtime enforcement.
# Debug UI draws a separate, hard-coded "healthy" queue diagram.
# Start with a single worker before adding global coordination.

issues.text: It checks CPU but ignores memory and capacity consumed by jobs started during the tick.
issues.why: Concurrent starts can exceed both the remaining CPU budget and the memory budget.

issues.text: Static priority and unlimited backfill can keep the build waiting.
issues.why: A reservation and an explicit fairness policy give the blocked work a future opportunity.

issues.text: Independent readers can claim the same global job.
issues.why: Reading is not ownership. A real distributed queue needs atomic claims and a recovery rule.

issues.text: Runtime estimates without enforcement can invalidate the reservation.
issues.why: Choose whether to stop overruns, reschedule reservations or isolate capacity; surface the breach.

issues.text: The diagram can show healthy state while the real queue is stuck.
issues.why: Generate observations from the actual decision and workload state.

issues.text: Beginning with one worker is itself a correctness bug.
issues.why: A single worker is a sensible bounded first step. Be clear about what it cannot prove.

build.title: A scheduler you can explain
build.brief:
Implement `select_jobs(now, capacity, running, pending)` and `visualize(...)`. All times are integer minutes; CPU and RAM are positive integers. IDs are unique. Running jobs have `cpu`, `ram`, and `end`; pending jobs have `id`, `cpu`, `ram`, `duration`, `priority`, and `submitted`. Running usage fits capacity. Durations are positive. Inputs follow this contract.

Reject jobs exceeding total capacity, returning their IDs sorted. Ignore future arrivals. Sort eligible jobs by descending `priority + (now - submitted) // 10`, then ascending submitted time, then ID. Completed jobs (`end <= now`) consume nothing. Start jobs that fit, subtracting CPU and RAM cumulatively.

Reserve only the first job that cannot start: find the earliest running-job end time at which it fits. Later jobs may start only if they fit now AND finish at or before that reservation. This is conservative EASY-style backfill protecting one head job, not Slurm’s complete algorithm. Return `{"start": [ids in start order], "reserved": {"id": id, "at": time} or None, "rejected": [ids]}`. Never mutate inputs.

`visualize` returns a JSON string with `now`, `capacity`, `running`, `pending`, and `plan`, calling your real scheduler to get the plan. The final test prints this snapshot. Inspect it against the expected resource releases.

tests.name: Cumulative CPU and RAM
Backfill at reservation boundary
Long backfill must wait
Reservation uses both resources
Aging and stable ties
Impossible requests do not block
Finished jobs release capacity; future jobs wait
Inputs are preserved and decisions repeat
Visualization reflects the real decision

hints: Write fits(job, at): count only allocations whose end is greater than at. Include jobs started in this tick.
Sort with a tuple: negative effective priority, submitted time, ID. Reject impossible jobs before making any reservation.
The reservation time must be one of the active job end times. Once set, allow later jobs only when now + duration <= reserved time.

ship.prompt: Write two lines: what changed and why, then the command or case a reviewer should run. Keep it to 60 words.
ship.coachFocus: Concrete behavior and reproducible evidence; mention the single-worker scope.
ship.example:
Reserve capacity for the waiting build while short jobs use the gap on one worker.
Test a 4-CPU build blocked until minute 5: the 5-minute agent starts, the 6-minute agent waits.

recall.q: A backfill task fits now but finishes after the head reservation. Under our conservative rule, what happens?
choices: Start it because CPU is free
recall.why: Protect the head job’s promised start. Our conservative exercise requires backfill to finish by that time.

recall.q: Two workers both read an available job. What prevents duplicate ownership?
choices: An atomic claim with a recovery protocol
recall.why: Reading an entry does not acquire it. Execution needs a claim, a lease/recovery rule and idempotent effects.

disclosure:
This is an authored exercise based on three video transcripts and the linked primary scheduling documents. The agent proposal contains deliberate mistakes. The scheduler is a single-machine teaching model; claims, retries and runtime enforcement belong in a real worker. Reading and design use self-assessment; test results measure only the cases shown. XP records practice, not job readiness or likely pay.

The briefing uses the same versioned visual system as every Proof mission. The optional local coach can be wrong. Your drafts and progress stay in this browser; opening sources and downloading Python or model assets makes network requests.
